lessons.au: R.K. Narayan (poem: Ruskin Bond – ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’)
lessons.words: sneer – speak in a very unkind way; frightful – unpleasant; face to face with – close to something and looking at it; reading it through – reading from beginning to end; crossly – a little angrily; mere skeleton – very thin; scowl – an angry look; tenacity – determination; cut in – interrupted at once; proposition – suggestion; mumble – say something not clearly; gloomily – in a way that things will not improve; sternly – seriously and strictly; tiptoed – walked quietly on toes; gesticulations – movements with hands and arms; snore – breathe noisily; apparition – ghost; scorpions – small poisonous creatures; slunk – moved quietly and secretly; laughing stock – object of ridicule; chum – a good friend; encased – covered closely; racked – made to suffer great pain; mortal weapon – deadly weapon; clutched – held tightly; burglar – a person who enters a building to steal; notorious – evil-minded; in a trice – very quickly; outcome – what actually happened; hold one’s peace – keep quiet; undaunted – without hesitation; chore – task; sherry – yellow or brown wine; upholding – making clear to the world
lessons.notes: Second form – seventh standard during British times. Poem ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’ is part of this unit.
ab: Before you read
Can you guess why ‘I’ smiled? At his ignorance / forgetfulness in general / ready wit? [Choose the most appropriate one]
Ready wit. The boy cleverly added ‘forget’ as the fifth feature, which made the father smile.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–5)
1. Swami’s father drew his attention to a report in the newspaper. What was the report about?

It was about a village lad who, while returning home by a jungle path, came face to face with a tiger. He fought the tiger and then stayed up a tree for half a day until people came and killed the tiger.

2. The report said that the boy stayed on the tree for half-a-day. Why did he do so? a. He wanted to watch the tiger from the top of a tree. b. He wanted someone to kill the tiger. c. He wanted to take rest for some time.
b. He wanted someone to kill the tiger. (He waited in the tree until people came and killed it.)
3. Swami said that a very strong and grown-up person might have fought with the tiger. Do you think he made this remark out of his (a) experience (b) wisdom (c) belief?
c. belief. Swami believed that strength and age make a person brave enough to fight a tiger.
4a. ‘Can you prove you have courage?’ Swami’s father said. Was he joking? Or, serious?
He was serious.
4b. Was it a challenge? Or, a command?
At first it was a challenge (‘Can you prove you have courage?’). It soon became a command: ‘You must sleep alone hereafter.’
5. The place where Swami usually slept was ……………………. (Fill in the blank)
in the passage, beside his granny.
6. What is disgraceful, according to Swami’s father?
It is disgraceful for Swami to sleep beside his granny or mother like a baby.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 6–9)
1. What do you think was the practice of granny before she went to bed?
Granny used to tell Swami a story before he went to sleep.
2. Was Swami really sleeping? Or, was he pretending?
He was pretending. He made signs to silence his granny and snored under the blanket to avoid talking and to escape from his father.
3. To Swami, his father looked like an ………………… (Fill in the blank)
apparition (ghost).
4. Why do you think Swami looked at his granny and his mother while following his father to the room?
He was pleading silently for help. He hoped one of them would stop his father from making him sleep alone in the office room.
5a. ‘There might be scorpions behind your law books,’ said Swami. Had he seen them earlier? Or, were there scorpions really?
He had not seen them. There were no scorpions; he was making an excuse.
5b. Was it a trick to escape from his father?
Yes. It was a trick to escape from sleeping alone in the office room.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 10–13)
1. Swami wished that the tiger hadn’t spared the boy, which means… a. he didn’t want the boy to be alive. b. he didn’t want the tiger to be alive.
a. he didn’t want the boy to be alive.
2. As silence deepened in the room, what was Swami reminded of?
He was reminded of the stories of devils and ghosts he had heard in his life.
3. Which place in the room did Swami think was safe, compact and reassuring?
The space under the bench.
4. Swami touched ……………………………………..in the room instead of granny. (Fill in the blank appropriately)
the wooden leg of the bench.
5. Swami saw a moving creature in the room. It was ………………… a. his shadow b. a scorpion c. a man
c. a man. It was the burglar hiding under the bench, though Swami thought it was a devil.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 14–17)
1. Who cried, ‘Aiyo! Something has bitten me’?
The burglar cried out.
2. Who did father, cook and a servant stumble upon?
The burglar lying amidst the furniture with a bleeding ankle.
3. Why were congratulations showered on Swami?
Because he had bitten one of the most notorious house-breakers of the district, and the police were grateful to him.
4. Do you think Swami really wanted to join the police? If not, what did he want to be?
No. He wanted to be an engine driver, a railway guard or a bus conductor.
5. Did Swami muster up courage to sleep alone after the burglar incident?
No. He went back to sleeping beside his granny in his usual place.
6. Who supported Swami – his mother or his granny?
His mother supported him. She said, ‘You let him sleep where he likes.’
Think about the text
1. A report about a boy in the newspaper was an unexpected event in Swami’s life. Justify.
The report led his father to challenge Swami to sleep alone in the office room. This changed Swami’s peaceful routine and forced him to face his fear of darkness.
2. Swami made a comment on the newspaper report. Was he right? How did his view differ from that of his father?

Swami felt that strength and age matter. His father felt that courage matters more than strength or age. Swami was partly right that strength helps, but his father was right that courage is essential. Accept reasoned answers.
3. What desperate attempts did Swami make to escape from his father?
He offered to sleep in the hall, claimed there were scorpions, asked for a lamp, asked the door to be left open, pleaded with his mother and granny, and pretended to be asleep.
4. Why did Swami conclude that his father’s proposition was frightful?
Sleeping alone in the dark office room, away from his granny, was frightening for him.
5. As the night advanced, Swami felt that something terrible would happen to him. What would it be? How would it happen?
He feared that devils or ghosts would come and carry him away. He thought the devil would come up, pull him out and tear him.
6. There was absolute silence in the room. In spite of it, some noises reached Swami’s ears. What were they?
The ticking of the clock, the rustle of trees, snoring sounds and night insects humming.
7. Narrate Swami’s dreadful experience when he was lying under the bench.

He had a nightmare in which a tiger chased him and his feet stuck to the ground. He woke up in fear, felt lonely and saw something moving. He believed a devil was coming to tear him, so he crawled out, hugged it and bit it with his teeth.
8. How was Swami honoured by his classmates, teacher and the headmaster?
His classmates looked at him with respect, his teacher patted his back, and the headmaster said he was a true scout.
9. Why did father want Swami to sleep alone in the office room?
He wanted Swami to overcome his fear of darkness, to learn to be brave and to cultivate good habits.
10. Who do you think was wiser, Swami or his father? Justify your preference.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: The father was wiser, as he tried to build courage and self-reliance in his son instead of letting him depend on his granny.
11. Why did Swami feel relieved at the end?
Because his father gave up the plan and let him sleep where he liked, so he could sleep beside his granny again.
12. Suppose you are Swami of the story. Write a brief letter to your friend describing how you helped to catch a burglar in your house.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample letter: Dear Ravi, I hope you are well. Last night a burglar entered our house. While he was hiding under the bench in my father’s office room, I bit his ankle. He cried out and my father, the cook and the servant caught him. The police were pleased and the headmaster praised me. Yours affectionately, Swami.
13. Put the words (caring, protective, innocent, tricky, authoritative, disciplined, helpless, nervous) in the appropriate columns: Swami’s father / Mother / Granny / Swami.
Swami’s father: authoritative, disciplined. Mother: protective. Granny: caring, innocent. Swami: tricky, nervous, helpless. (Accept reasoned placements.)

1. Why do you think the audience, on hearing the dialogue, burst into laughter?
The actor mixed up the words, saying ‘stars were barking, dogs were twinkling’ and ‘the thief broke the clock and took away the wall’, which was ridiculous and funny.
2. Try to repeat the words as delivered by the actor.
‘Stars were barking, dogs were twinkling, and the thief broke the clock and took away the wall.’ (Accept the learner’s attempt.)

Speak well – Language function: Refusing invitation
Imagine that Swami receives advice from his father and granny. How would Swami say that he accepts or refuses it? Write a dialogue using the expressions given.

Granny: ‘Would you like to hear a story tonight?’ Swami: ‘Thank you for the offer, Granny. I think, on the whole, I’d rather not. Thank you all the same.’ (refusing)
Read and respond
Task 1: Mr. Khanna was surprised at the astrologer’s prediction. What made him feel so?
The astrologer knew details of his family, such as his children, his shopping and his ration card, which made Khanna feel impressed.
Task 1: Why wasn’t the astrologer able to predict Mr. Khanna’s future?
The astrologer only knew facts about the past and present which he had gathered, and he could not truly predict the future.
Task 1: In the conversation, who do you think has better common sense?
Accept reasoned answers. Mr. Khanna, as he realised that the astrologer’s knowledge was based on ordinary facts.
Task 2: Which word in the passage gives the opposite meaning of what was meant to be said?
‘hardly’ – it should have been ‘hard’. ‘Worked hardly’ means barely worked, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.

2. The files are heavy. I’ll carry them for you. (Begin with ‘would’) Function: Offering help

Make reference – Dictionary
Task 1: Based on the entries of ‘lorry’ and ‘truck’, what do the entries tell us?

a. lorry is a word used in British English. b. In British English truck means an open railway vehicle, not a motor vehicle. c. In American English truck means a motor vehicle, the same as lorry. d. truck can also mean a simple hand-pulled or hand-pushed cart in both British and American English.
Task 2: What does ‘derog’ mean in the entry for ‘windbag’?
‘derog’ means derogatory. The word windbag is insulting, so a person may feel offended if called a windbag.
Task 3: With the help of a dictionary, find out what you can understand about: 1. cheque and check as nouns. 2. hire and rent as verbs.

Cheque: a written order to a bank to pay money. Check (noun): examination or verification; in American English, the bill in a restaurant. Hire (verb): pay to use something temporarily or to employ someone. Rent (verb): pay to use something owned by another person.

POETRY – Before you read (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
a–c. Childish habits given: marbles, kites, bike riding. d–e. Add more.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: Playing hopscotch; eating candies; singing rhymes.
Understand the poem (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
1. The speaker does not call his grandmother ‘childish’. What else was she according to him? Why? (lines 1–4)
She was a genius, because she could climb trees, spreading or high, and was up their branches in a trice.
2. Identify the lines that suggest that grandma had been in the habit of climbing trees for a long period.
‘Ever since childhood, she’d had this gift’ (line 5) and ‘Having learned to climb from a loving brother when she was six’ (line 13).
3. Look at lines 7 and 8. Who do you think would tell her so?
Her family members, such as her children or relatives, would tell her that climbing should stop when one grew old.
4. Do you find anything odd in the reply given by the grandma? Why? (lines 10–11)
Yes. Instead of growing old gracefully she says she will ‘grow disgracefully’, which is an odd and playful reply.
5. Others had feared that granny would fall one day. Did this happen? Or did something else happen? (lines 15–18)
She did not fall, but while the family was in town she climbed a tree and could not come down. She had to be rescued.
6. What had the doctor recommended? What was the reaction of the kids?
The doctor recommended a quiet week in bed. The kids were relieved and tucked her up well.
7. Quote the lines which suggest how wholeheartedly granny enjoyed climbing a tree.
‘happier in a tree than in a lift’ (line 6) and ‘She’d be up their branches in a trice’ (line 2).
8. ‘My dad knew his duties.’ What did he think his duty was?
He thought it was his duty to fulfil his mother’s wish and build her a house in a treetop.
9. Look at the picture given below the title. Quote the lines that might have guided the artist to draw that.
(ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ) ‘Made her a tree-house with windows and a door’ and ‘She sits there in state and drinks sherry with me’ may have guided the artist.
Read and appreciate (Grandma Climbs a Tree)
A1. Does the behaviour of grandma strike you as unusual? Support your view quoting her ways and responses.
Yes. Way 1: Grandma climbing a tree at sixty-two. Response: ‘Well I’ll grow disgracefully, I can do it better.’ Response: She asked for a house in a treetop instead of staying in bed.
A2. Discuss whether what the grandma was doing was graceful or otherwise.
Accept reasoned answers. Her climbing was not graceful by usual standards, but it was graceful in spirit because it gave her joy and independence.
A3. Both the narrator and his father were considerate towards Grandma. Substantiate with textual support.
The narrator tucked her up well and the father said, ‘You’ll have what you want, dear. I’ll start work tonight.’ He built a tree-house with windows and a door.
A4. If you were to divide the poem into two parts, which line would you pick as the beginning of the second part? Why?
‘The outcome was different – while we were in town’ (line 17). From here the poem shifts from the climbing to the accident and its aftermath.
B1. Write at least 5 pairs of rhyming words.
gift – lift; town – down; stronger – longer; undaunted – wanted; tonight – right.
B2. ‘It was like a brief season’ – name the figure of speech. What are the two things compared?
Simile (‘like’). Her confinement to bed is compared to a season in hell, showing how painful it was for her.
B3. ‘For being happier in a tree than in a lift’. What is suggested through this line?
She loved nature and freedom more than comfort and convenience; she enjoyed the outdoors more than modern comforts.
B4. Rewrite without using ‘not’: ‘There was not a tree she hadn’t been up.’ Give examples of double negatives.
She had been up every tree in the garden. Double negatives examples: ‘It is not impossible that he will come.’ ‘She is not unkind.’ ‘I could not help but laugh.’

qb.a: Father, cook and servant came with a light, fell on the burglar and caught him.

qb.q: Describe/Narrate Swami’s dreadful experience when he was lying under the bench.
qb.a: He crept under the bench, covered himself with the blanket and fell asleep. He dreamt a tiger chased him, groaned in despair, touched the wooden leg of the bench, thought a devil would pull him out, and when it came near, he crawled, hugged it and used his teeth as a mortal weapon.

qb.q: a) Who is the speaker? (‘I think he must have been a very strong and grown-up person…’)
qb.a: Swami.

qb.q: b) What does the speaker mean? (same extract)
qb.a: He means the newspaper report was wrong, as a boy could not fight a tiger; a grown-up person must have done it.

qb.q: c) What was important according to the speaker?
qb.a: According to the speaker both strength and age were important.

qb.q: a) Who posed the challenge: ‘Leave alone strength, can you prove that you have courage?’ b) How did the speaker want the ‘you’ to prove courage? c) What was his view on courage?
qb.a: a) Swami’s father. b) By sleeping alone in the office room. c) Courage is more important than strength or age.

qb.q: a) Who had to sleep alone? (‘From the first of the next month, I’ll sleep alone father.’) b) Why? c) What reply did he get?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) To escape from his father’s challenge. c) His father insisted he should sleep alone from that day itself.

qb.q: a) Who did the ‘you’ usually sleep with? (‘You must sleep alone hereafter.’) b) Where was Swami asked to sleep? c) Why?
qb.a: a) His granny. b) In his father’s office room. c) To prove his courage.

qb.q: a) Who is the speaker of ‘Why do you disturb him?’ b) Who was disturbing him? c) Why did he say so?
qb.a: a) Swami’s granny. b) Swami’s father. c) Father was waking Swami up to make him sleep alone in the office room.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘There may be scorpions behind your law books’? b) When? c) What made him say so?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) When his father took him to the office room to sleep alone that night. c) It was an excuse to escape sleeping alone.

qb.q: a) Who is the ‘you’ in ‘I’ll make you the laughing stock of your school’? b) Who wanted this? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) Swami’s father. c) To prevent Swami from moving to his granny’s side in the middle of the night.

qb.q: a) Who cried ‘Aiyo! Something has bitten me’? b) What caused the cry? c) When?
qb.a: a) The burglar. b) Swami bit him. c) When Swami hugged his leg and bit him with his teeth.

qb.q: a) Who gave the suggestion ‘Why don’t you join the police?’ b) Why? c) What did Swami want to become?
qb.a: a) The police inspector. b) Swami caught a notorious burglar. c) Swami wanted to become a railway guard, engine driver or bus conductor.

qb.q: a) Who wanted a lamp? (‘Can I have a lamp burning in the room?’) b) Why? c) Whom did he ask?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) He was afraid of darkness. c) His father.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘her’ refer to? (‘Tell her so and don’t look at me.’) b) Who should tell her and what? c) What reply did the speaker get?
qb.a: a) Swami’s granny. b) Swami’s father should tell his mother that it was not the proper way to bring up Swami. c) Father replied the statement was not directed at the speaker.

qb.q: a) Who is ‘he’ in ‘He wished that the tiger had not spared the boy’? b) When? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) When he was forced to sleep alone in the office room. c) If the tiger had killed the boy, there would be no report and no forced sleeping.

qb.q: a) Who is ‘I’ in ‘You are in the second form and I don’t like the way you are being brought up’? b) Who was in second form? c) When?
qb.a: a) Swami’s father. b) Swami. c) When Swami was trying to escape his father’s proposition.

qb.q: a) Who is the ‘me’ in ‘Our captain has asked me to tell you’? b) What had the captain asked him to tell? c) When?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) That they were buying new bats and balls and admitting elders to the cricket club. c) When he tried to divert his father from the challenge.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘he’ refer to? (‘He knew his father’s tenacity at such moments.’) b) When? c) What does ‘tenacity’ mean?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) When his father pulled him out of bed to take him to the office room. c) Determination.

qb.q: a) Who is the speaker of ‘He didn’t have a wink of sleep the whole of last night’? b) When? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Swami’s mother. b) The day after the heroic incident, when Swami’s father enquired about him. c) He had slept alone in the office room and was afraid of darkness.

qb.q: a) Who is the speaker of ‘You let him sleep where he likes, you needn’t risk his life again’? b) What risk? c) When?
qb.a: a) Swami’s mother. b) Risking his life by sleeping alone in the office room. c) After father returned and saw Swami in his usual place.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘you’ refer to in ‘All right, molly-coddle and spoil him’? b) How was he spoiled? c) What does ‘molly-coddle’ mean?
qb.a: a) Swami’s mother. b) He slept beside his granny; mother and granny did not advise him to learn to sleep alone and be courageous. c) To treat someone very kindly and protect them too much.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘his’ refer to in ‘his heart beat faster’? b) Where was he? c) Why did his heart beat faster?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) In the office room. c) He was afraid of darkness and sleeping alone there.

qb.q: a) Who asked ‘How could a boy fight a tiger?’ b) When? c) Who else could fight a tiger, according to the speaker?
qb.a: a) Swami. b) When he heard the news of a village lad fighting a tiger. c) A very strong and grown-up person.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘I hardly know anything about the boy’? b) Who is the boy? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Swami’s mother. b) Swami. c) Swami’s father complained about Swami’s upbringing.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘We’ll see about that later’? b) To whom? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Swami’s father. b) To Swami. c) Swami tried to escape the proposition of sleeping alone by changing the topic.

qb.q: Write a paragraph using the given clues: profile of R. K. Narayan (Name, Date of Birth, Place of Birth, Education, Father, Spouse, Profession, Books).
qb.a: This is the profile of R. K. Narayan, born on 10 October 1906 in Madras. He studied at Maharaja College, Mysore. His father was R. V. Krishnaswami Iyer and his wife was Rajam. He was an English novelist. His books include Malgudi Days, A Tiger for Malgudi, The Guide and Swami and his Friends.

qb.q: 67. Develop the story from the clues: three friends (two geese and a tortoise) decide to migrate; geese carry the tortoise with a stick held by their beaks; the tortoise is told not to speak; children clap; the tortoise bursts out and falls.
qb.a: The geese devised a way to carry the tortoise by holding a stick in their beaks, warning it not to speak. Children clapped, the tortoise got angry and burst out, and fell down.

qb.q: 67(ii). Develop the story: tortoise and hare argue about a race; the hare sleeps; the tortoise reaches the goal and wins. Moral.
qb.a: The hare ran fast but slept midway; the tortoise ran slowly and steadily, reached the goal and won. Moral: slow and steady wins the race.

qb.q: 67(iii). Develop the story: a miser loses a purse with a thousand rupees, an honest farmer returns it, the miser claims it had 1100 rupees, and the judge rules for the farmer.
qb.a: The farmer returned the purse; the miser claimed the reward was already taken since the purse had 1100 rupees. The judge ruled the purse was not the miser’s, as he claimed it had 1100 rupees, and asked the farmer to keep it until the real owner came.

qb.q: 68. Study the given picture and write a description of what it suggests.
qb.a: Accept picture-based description (e.g. circus scene, beach scene with boats and fishermen, village scene, or children flying kites).
qb.chk: Check picture: picture-based item; verify numbering from the picture

qb.q: 69(i)a. What kind of a boy was Lal Bahadur?
qb.a: Brave and kind; he was short and thin but full of courage and vitality.

qb.q: 69(i)b. Why did the vendor sell all his mangoes for one anna?
qb.a: Lal Bahadur said a hundred mangoes for one anna was too cheap, so he gave the vendor one anna instead of half an anna. (Key: the vendor sold cheaply because it was getting dark and he wanted to go home.)

qb.q: 69(ii)a. How is the abacus useful?
qb.a: It is the earliest form of mechanical computer; calculations can be made quickly.

qb.q: 69(ii)b. How are calculations done on an abacus?
qb.a: By moving coloured beads up and down on parallel rods in a wooden frame.

qb.q: 69(iii)a. Why did the people lock their doors and shut the windows?
qb.a: They heard the roar of a leopard and were afraid.

qb.q: 69(iii)b. How did Sunita send the leopard back to the forest?
qb.a: She picked up a hen from the yard and threw it towards the leopard; the hungry leopard took it and ran into the forest.

qb.q: ‘Aiyo! Something has bitten me.’ Why did the speaker make an agonized, thundering cry?
o: he fell over the heavy furniture.
someone suddenly turned on the light.
he was caught by the family members.

qb.q: Based on the passage, the people who rushed into the room with lights were
o: A burglar, father, and a servant

qb.q: The phrase ‘tumbling and falling amidst furniture’ suggests that
o: The burglar was trying to rearrange the furniture.
The room was empty and dark.
There was a sudden, chaotic struggle or accident in the dark.
The family members fell down as soon as they entered.

qb.q: The statement that is true according to the passage is
o: The burglar successfully escaped from the room.
The three people who came in helped the burglar to stand up.
The burglar was caught as he was injured and lying among the furniture.
The cook was the first person to attack the burglar.

qb.q: Swami found the proposition ‘frightful’ as
o: he was afraid of his father's cricket captain.
it meant changing his usual routine of sleeping next to his grandmother.
he did not want to join the new cricket club.
he was terrified of sleeping alone in the passage.

qb.q: Whenever his sleeping arrangement was altered, Swami felt
o: Excited and eager to stay awake
Shivering with fear and unable to sleep
Angry and argumentative with his father

qb.q: The phrase ‘with a great deal of enthusiasm’ suggests that Swami
o: was genuinely thrilled to share the sports news with his father.
was trying hard to distract his father from the terrifying topic of sleeping alone.
wanted to show off his position as the captain of the team.
was celebrating a recent victory in a cricket match.

qb.q: 70. Narrate how a coward boy, Swami, became a hero overnight (8–10 sentences).
qb.a: The newspaper carried a report of a brave village lad who fought a tiger. Swami could not accept that a boy could do this, and his father challenged him to sleep alone in the office room. Swami, with fear of devils, saw something moving in the dark and thought his end had come. As an attempt for survival he hugged it with all his might and used his teeth as a mortal weapon. It was a burglar, and Swami became a hero overnight.

qb.q: 71. Write an essay on Global Warming (or Social Media / National Symbols).
qb.a: Global warming is caused by increased greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and industry. It raises temperatures, sea levels and causes climate change, and harms ecosystems and health. We should use renewable energy, plant trees, follow sustainable agriculture and cooperate internationally.

qb.q: 72. Write a letter to the municipal officer to provide a drinking water facility in your locality (Suhas/Saritha, GHS Narayanapura).
qb.a: Sub: Request to provide water facility in our area. I am a resident of Gandhi Colony. The pipeline was laid six months ago but no water flows; residents must buy water and the poor cannot afford it. I request you to provide a proper water facility at the earliest. Yours faithfully.

qb.q: 1. The poet does not call his grandmother ‘childish’. What else was she, according to him? Why?
qb.a: She was a genius, because she could climb trees, spreading or high, and was up their branches in a trice even at sixty-two.

qb.q: 2. Quote the lines that show grandma had been in the habit of climbing trees for a long period.
qb.a: ‘Ever since childhood, she’d had this gift’ (line 5) and ‘Having learned to climb from a loving brother when she was six’ (line 13).

qb.q: 3. What did the neighbours advise Ruskin Bond’s grandma? How did she respond?
qb.a: They advised her to stop climbing as she grew old and to grow old gracefully. She laughed and said she preferred to grow old disgracefully.

qb.q: 4. Others feared that granny would fall from a tree one day. Did this happen?
qb.a: No. But one day when the family was in town she climbed a tree and could not come down; she was rescued with great difficulty.

qb.q: 5. What did the doctor recommend grandma? What was the reaction of the kids?
qb.a: The doctor recommended a week’s bed rest. The kids sighed with relief that she would not climb trees and risk her life.

qb.q: 6. ‘My dad knew his duties.’ What did the speaker think his father’s duty was?
qb.a: His duty was to fulfil his mother’s wish; he built a tree-house for her with the poet’s help.

qb.q: 7. Both the poet and his father were considerate towards Grandma. Substantiate.
qb.a: They built a tree-house with windows and a door for her. The father said, ‘You’ll have what you want, dear. I’ll start work tonight.’ The poet tucked her in well.

qb.q: 8. How did grandma feel while she was resting in bed?
qb.a: Miserable. For her, a week in bed was like a brief season in hell, as she loved to look at the dancing leaves.

qb.q: 9. What qualities of grandma do you appreciate?
qb.a: Accept reasoned answers: her passion, courage, independence, and joy in living her own way.

qb.q: How did grandma fulfil her wish in the poem ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’?
qb.a: After her recovery from the week of bed rest, she demanded a house on a tree. The poet’s dutiful father built a tree-house with windows and a door, with the poet’s help, so that she could live in a tree and uphold her right to do so.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘she’ refer to? b) What was the gift she had? c) Where was she happier?
qb.a: a) The poet’s grandma. b) Climbing any type of tree. c) In a tree than in a lift.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘Well, I’ll grow disgracefully, I can do it better’? b) What was disgraceful? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Granny, to her friends and neighbours/advisers. b) Climbing trees as she grew old. c) She had a passion for climbing trees and would be happier doing it.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘all’ refer to? b) Why did they fear a terrible fall? c) What was the outcome?
qb.a: a) People. b) They feared she would fall, being old. c) She climbed a tree but could not come down; she was rescued.

qb.q: a) Who is the ‘I’ in ‘I strongly recommend her, a quiet week in bed’? b) Why? c) Response?
qb.a: a) The doctor. b) Because granny had high fever. c) The kids felt relief that she would not climb trees.

qb.q: a) What was ‘like a brief season in hell’? b) Why was it like hell? c) What would be like heaven to her?
qb.a: a) A week in bed. b) Granny wanted to climb and stay on trees, so bed rest felt like hell. c) Climbing trees.

qb.q: Write a paragraph describing the picture of traditional farming (harvesting in a paddy field).
qb.a: Accept description from the picture: female workers harvesting crops, male farmers threshing grain on a platform, coconut and areca groves, tiled-roof houses and a distant mountain range.

qb.q: Summarize the poem ‘Grandma Climbs a Tree’ in your own words.
qb.a: Ruskin Bond calls his grandmother a genius because she climbed trees at sixty-two, learned from her brother at six, and ignored advice. Once she was stuck in a tree and rescued; the doctor ordered a week’s bed rest, which was like hell to her. She then demanded a tree-house, which her dutiful son built with the poet’s help, so she lived happily in it.

qb.q: 18. How was grandma successful in fulfilling her desire to live in a tree house?
qb.a: After the bed rest she demanded a tree-house; her dutiful son built it with the poet’s help, so she could live in a tree and uphold her right to do so.

qb.q: 19. Both the poet and his father were considerate towards grandmother. Substantiate with textual support.
qb.a: When she recovered and asked for a tree-house, the father built it with windows and doors. The poet climbed up to her room every day with glasses and a tray and drank sherry with her.

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Passive) The burglar ______ by Swami. [Swami caught the burglar]
qb.a: was caught

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Passive) A story ______ by granny. [Granny was telling a story]
qb.a: was being told

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Passive) A new bag ______ by Janaki in the shop. [Janaki has purchased a new bag]
qb.a: has been purchased

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Passive) Answers ______ by Krishna. [Krishna is evaluating answers]
qb.a: are being evaluated

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Comparative) Swami was ______ than any other boy in the class. [the cleverest boy]
qb.a: cleverer

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Comparative) Seema is ______ than any other girl in the family. [the tallest girl]
qb.a: taller

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Comparative) Rose is ______ than any other flower. [the most attractive flower]
qb.a: more attractive

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Comparative) The Pacific is ______ than any other ocean in the world. [the deepest ocean]
qb.a: deeper

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Reported) Swami complained to his father that his office room ______ dusty.
qb.a: was

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Reported) Burglar cried that something ______ bitten him.
qb.a: had

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Correction) Congratulations were showered on Swami, the next day. His classmates ______ at him with respect. (verb)
qb.a: looked

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Correction) Swami ______ got up and spread his bed under the bench. (adverb)
qb.a: hurriedly

qb.q: Fill in the blank: (Correction) Swami’s father sat ______ gazing at the newspaper on his lap. (adverb)
qb.a: gloomily

qb.a: How

qb.a: Why

lessons.t: There’s a Girl by the Tracks!
lessons.au: Deven Kanal (poem: William Shakespeare – ‘Quality of Mercy’, for memorization)
lessons.words: suburban – of a place outside a city; commuter – one who travels to work daily; swarm – rush; hurtle – move fast; tenuous – weak or shaky; panic – suddenly feel frightened; clattering – making a loud sound; muffled – silenced; thud – low sound; gasp – deep breath taken when surprised; emanate – come from; impulsively – without thinking; frantically – with no hope; wary – worried; shove – push roughly; sprint – run very fast; sprawled – lie stretched; gash – deep cut; gingerly – nervously; implore – request; fiancé – man a woman is engaged to; lanky – tall and thin; treading water – making no progress; to grind out – say with effort; black out – become unconscious; hang around – wait; suture – stitch; barely speak – not able to speak; partly sedated – half awake due to drugs; strain’d – forced; droppeth – drops; blest – blessed; sceptre – decorated rod of a king; temporal – worldly; majesty – royal power; doth – does; dread – threat; enthroned – seated; attribute – quality; likest – like; seasons – tempers
lessons.notes: Mumbai local train incident, December 2010. Quality of Mercy is a memorization poem from Shakespeare’s ‘The Merchant of Venice’.
ab: Before you read
1. If you had been there at the place shown in the picture, how would you have reacted? (Begin with ‘I would have’)
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಚಿತ್ರ ನೋಡಿ) Sample: I would have immediately rushed to help the injured person and called for help.
images/class-10/english/c10-en-sem1-l02-accident-picture.webp
Imagine you lent money to your friend who doesn’t return it when you need it. What would you do? (a. forgive b. punish c. ignore d. pity e. sympathize f. other)
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: I would sympathize with him and gently remind him to return it when he can.
2. Which quality of Baleshwar strikes you as great?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: His courage and compassion in helping a stranger without any hesitation.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–5)
1. ‘It’s a regular scene.’ What was regular about the scene? (para 1)
Commuters rush in and out of the packed suburban train at every halt, squeezing into crowded coaches.
2. Roma tried to settle into a corner near the door. Was she right in doing this? What would you have done?
Accept reasoned answers. She was not wise, as standing near an open door in a packed train is unsafe. Sample: I would have held a firm handrail and moved to a safer place inside the coach.
3. ‘There’s a girl by the tracks!’ the voices cried out. Whose voices do you think those were?
The voices of the passengers in Baleshwar’s train, who had seen the girl lying beside the tracks.
4. Baleshwar was impulsive in taking a decision because ……………………… (para 3)
he could not bear to see a young woman lying injured by the tracks and wanted to save her immediately.
5. The dictionary says ‘callous’ means ‘unconcerned’. In this situation, who were ‘callous’ towards the accident?
The passengers in Baleshwar’s compartment, who did not volunteer to help because they were afraid of getting involved.
6. Identify two more verbs or verbal phrases in paragraph 5 that describe Baleshwar’s movement.
‘jumped off’ and ‘sprint back’ (also ‘shoved himself’ is given).
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 6–9)
1. Where did Baleshwar find Roma at last?
He found her sprawled by the side of the tracks, between two stations about five kilometres apart in Thane district.
2. ‘Behenji, aap theek hai?’ But there was no response and no help in sight. Why was it so? (para 6)
Roma was unconscious and badly injured, and they were alone in an isolated place between two stations, with no one nearby to help.
3. Fill in the table with appropriate details.

Roma Talreja: Age 21; Education: B.Com graduate; State: Maharashtra (from Pune); Profession: call centre executive; Reason for boarding the train: going home after her shift. Baleshwar Mishra: Age 20; Education: high-school dropout; State: Uttar Pradesh (from Mirzapur); Profession: unemployed, looking for a job; Reason for boarding the train: going home after spending the day with a friend.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 10–14)
1. Who volunteered to help Baleshwar?
The middle-aged tempo-truck driver who spoke Gujarati stopped and helped him.
2. ‘Roma stirred and her eyes fluttered open.’ What could have made her react so?
The jolt of the truck moving forward made her stir and open her eyes.
3. Fill in the columns about Dinesh (para 14).
Name: Dinesh Talreja; Job: marketing job at a retail outlet; Place: Ulhasnagar; Vehicle: motorcycle.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 15–20)
1. ‘Oh, I couldn’t thank him,’ Baleshwar thought. Who do you think he couldn’t thank?
The truck driver, who had slipped away with his truck after helping.
2. Why did Baleshwar revisit the spot where Roma had fallen?
He wanted to look for Roma’s belongings, as Dinesh had said her cell phone and handbag were missing.
3. Baleshwar got some assurance from a railway employee. What was that?
The employee assured him that some of Roma’s belongings had been found.
4. Roma said, ‘I think it’s astonishing’. What was astonishing?
That a stranger would jump off a train and risk his life to save her.
Think about the text

1. Put the incidents relating to Roma in the right order: a. Roma lost her foothold. b. The train hurtled ahead. c. Roma was thrown out of the coach. d. Roma was jammed between two women. e. Roma panicked.
d, b, a, e, c
2. Set Baleshwar’s actions in the right sequence: a. crossed the track. b. carried the girl. c. saw the girl bleeding. d. requested motorists to help. e. prayed silently.
c, e, b, a, d
3. Write briefly the personal details (qualification and profession) of Roma Talreja and Baleshwar Mishra.
Roma Talreja: B.Com graduate from Pune, call centre executive. Baleshwar Mishra: high-school dropout from Mirzapur, UP, unemployed (looking for a job).
4. ‘Take the girl to Airoli,’ suggested the cop. But Baleshwar disagreed. Why?
Airoli was at least 10 km away, while Baleshwar knew of a closer hospital.

5. Arrange the incidents of paragraph 12 in sequence: a. The on-duty physician advised moving Roma to a nearby hospital. b. Baleshwar and Roma arrived at a small hospital. c. The nurses helped take the young woman in. d. The hospital lacked facilities and personnel.
b, c, d, a
6. Was Baleshwar right in asking Roma her name while she lay in a critical condition? Justify.
Yes. Asking her name and her brother’s number helped him check that she was conscious and get help for her family.
7. ‘Baleshwar had a good memory.’ Do you agree? Give examples.
Yes. He memorized Dinesh’s cell phone number even while Roma was fading out, and later he returned to the spot to look for her belongings.
8. The doctor at Divine Multi-Speciality Hospital admitted Roma without formalities. What made him do so?
He saw the extent of her injuries, which were serious, so he admitted her to the ICU immediately.
9. If Baleshwar had not come forward to help Roma, what would have happened to her?
According to Dr. Agarwal, she could have bled to death.
10. How did the truck driver help Baleshwar?
He stopped, helped lay Roma in the back of his truck, and drove them to the hospital.
11. Baleshwar felt that people of Mumbai were afraid. What were they afraid of?
They feared getting trapped in the courts or with the police.
12. The Dalai Lama says, ‘Love and compassion are the true religions to me…’ Does this relate to the lesson? How?
Yes. Baleshwar showed compassion for a stranger without any expectation of reward and without thinking of religion, caste or the risk to himself.

Understand the poem (Quality of Mercy)
1. Mercy is compared to something in the first two lines. What is it? How is this comparison apt? Justify.
Mercy is compared to the gentle rain from heaven. It is apt because mercy falls softly and quietly, and it refreshes and nourishes the one who receives it, just as rain nourishes the earth below.
2. The speaker says that mercy is twice blessed. What does she mean by this?
Mercy blesses both the one who gives it and the one who receives it.
3. ‘Sceptre shows the force of temporal power’. In contrast, what or whose quality does mercy stand for?
Mercy stands for the quality of compassion and kindness, which is a divine (God-like) attribute, above worldly power.
4. Classify the qualities into temporal power and divine attributes: love, revenge, sympathy, tyranny, cruelty, miserliness, mercy, hatred, tit-for-tat attitude, compassion.
Temporal power: revenge, tyranny, cruelty, miserliness, hatred, tit-for-tat attitude. Divine attributes: love, sympathy, mercy, compassion.
Read and appreciate (Quality of Mercy)
1. Read the first two lines. Explain the simile briefly.
Mercy is compared to gentle rain that falls from heaven on the earth below. As rain benefits everything beneath it, mercy benefits everyone.
2. How do you interpret the speaker’s view of mercy as twice blessed?
It blesses the giver, who gains the joy of helping, and the receiver, who is relieved of suffering.
3. The speaker says mercy is the mightiest of the mightiest. How does she justify this?
Mercy is enthroned in the heart of kings and is an attribute of God himself. It softens justice and makes earthly power show likeness to God’s power, which makes it mightier than the sceptre.

qb.a: a) Baleshwar. b) My brother Dinesh. c) To become unconscious.

qb.q: a) Who made the request ‘Chacha can I borrow your mobile?’ b) Who is Chacha? c) Why?
qb.a: a) Baleshwar. b) The Gujarati tempo truck driver. c) To call and inform Dinesh Talreja about Roma.

qb.q: a) Who does ‘I’ refer to in ‘a stranger would jump off a train and risk his life for me’? b) Who was the stranger? c) How did he help?
qb.a: a) Roma Talreja. b) Baleshwar Mishra. c) He jumped off the moving train, took her to a hospital and saved her life.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘I am new to Mumbai, but I’ve noticed that people here are afraid’? b) When? c) Why were people afraid?
qb.a: a) Baleshwar Mishra. b) When neither passengers nor passers-by helped to save Roma. c) They feared getting trapped in courts or with the police.

qb.q: a) Who was new to Mumbai? b) Why did he come? c) What made him feel the people were afraid?
qb.a: a) Baleshwar Mishra. b) He came in search of a job. c) No one came forward to help Roma when she fell, and no passer-by stopped to help him.

qb.q: a) Who asked ‘What’s your name?’ b) Whom was it asked to? c) When?
qb.a: a) Baleshwar. b) Roma Talreja. c) When the vehicle lurched forward, Roma stirred and opened her eyes.

qb.q: a) Who said ‘I am on the way’? b) To whom? c) How did he go there?
qb.a: a) Dinesh Talreja. b) Baleshwar Mishra. c) By his motorcycle.

qb.q: Write a paragraph using the clues: profile of Roma Talreja (21 years, 5 ft 2 in, 50 kg, B.Com, call centre executive, Maharashtra).
qb.a: This is the profile of Roma Talreja. She is 21 years old and five feet two inches tall, weighing 50 kg. She is a B.Com graduate working as a call centre executive. She belongs to Maharashtra.

qb.q: Develop the story using the clues: two notorious thieves enter a rich man’s house, find the safe open, pile up gold, silver and money, a man with a gun appears, the thieves try to escape but in vain, and the man calls the police.
qb.a: Two notorious thieves on the lookout for prey considered themselves clever and entered a rich man’s house to find the safe open. Happy with their luck, they piled up gold, silver and money. Suddenly the lights came on and a man with a gun appeared. The thieves tried to escape but in vain, and the man called the police, who sent them to jail. Moral: crime does not pay.

qb.q: Give a short account (2–3 sentences) of the picture: a village market with vendors selling fruits and vegetables, buyers, houses and a lake.
qb.a: Accept picture-based description: vendors sell fruits and vegetables to many men and women; a few houses, trees and a lake are behind them.

qb.q: a) What are the benefits of having a balanced diet? b) What types of food should be included?
qb.a: a) Maintains healthy weight, supports energy levels, reduces the risk of chronic diseases. b) Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins and healthy fats.

qb.q: a) What is discipline and why is it important? b) How does discipline benefit individuals?
qb.a: a) Adhering to rules or a code of conduct; it helps achieve goals and an organized life. b) It helps prioritize tasks, manage time and develop good habits, leading to personal and professional success.

qb.q: What qualities of Baleshwar do you like the most? (4 marks)
qb.a: Accept reasoned answers. Baleshwar showed compassion and courage: he jumped off a moving train to save a stranger, risking his life, and served Roma selflessly though she was a stranger to him.

qb.q: ‘Love and compassion are the true religions to me’ says Dalai Lama. Justify with reference to the lesson.
qb.a: Yes. Baleshwar, new to Mumbai, did not know Roma but jumped off the moving train out of love and compassion, carried her to hospital and saved her life. His selfless service shows that love and compassion are true religions.

qb.q: Write an essay on any one: a) Air pollution b) Mobile phones c) Need of moral education.
qb.a: Model essays are in the LBA key: air pollution (causes, health effects, need to plant trees and save planet), mobile phones (uses, addiction, misuse, judicious use), and moral education (character, critical thinking, respect and compassion; starts at home and school).

qb.q: Write a letter to your headmaster requesting help to pay a friend’s school fees (or other given letter).
qb.a: Model: Akash, student of X Std, writes to the Headmaster requesting help to pay fees for his friend Amar Pal, whose father has cancer and whose mother is a teacher; he thanks the headmaster for his help.

qb.q: Read the paragraph: ‘There’s a closer place I know of,’ said Baleshwar. The on-duty physician was unable to provide comprehensive treatment because
o: He was not qualified to treat the patient.
The hospital lacked the necessary personnel and equipment.
The patient arrived too late for medical intervention.
Baleshwar insisted on moving her to another facility.

qb.q: 1. Mercy is compared to gentle rain from heaven. How is this comparison apt?
qb.a: As gentle rain falls on the earth and blesses it, mercy falls on the one who receives it and blesses both giver and receiver.

qb.q: 2. How does the speaker justify that mercy is twice blessed?
qb.a: It blesses the giver (who gains joy in helping) and the receiver (who is relieved of suffering).

qb.q: 3. Sceptre shows the force of temporal power. In contrast, what quality does mercy stand for?
qb.a: Mercy stands for divine quality: compassion and kindness, which is above worldly power.

qb.q: 4. The poem has fourteen lines but it is not a sonnet. Justify.
qb.a: It has no rhyme scheme and does not follow the sonnet pattern of an octave and sestet, or three quatrains and a couplet.

qb.q: 6. a) What is compared to gentle rain from heaven? b) What blesses twice? c) Why does it bless twice?
qb.a: a) Mercy. b) Mercy. c) Both the one who shows mercy and the one who receives it are blessed.

qb.q: 7. a) What is a sceptre? b) How does it show temporal power? c) What quality does mercy stand for?
qb.a: a) A decorated rod carried by a king. b) It creates fear and awe among people. c) Divine quality which flows from the heart.

qb.q: 8. ’Tis mightiest in the mightiest. a) What do the two mightiest stand for? b) Meaning of mightiest? c) Intention?
qb.a: a) Mercy and a king. b) Most powerful. c) Mercy is more powerful than the power of a king.

qb.q: 9. It blesseth him that gives, and him that takes. a) What is ‘it’? b) How does it bless the giver? c) How does it bless the receiver?
qb.a: a) Mercy. b) The giver gets the blessing for having helped. c) The receiver is blessed by receiving the gift of mercy.

qb.q: 10. Mercy is above the sceptred sway. a) What is a sceptre? b) How is mercy above it? c) Which is above the sceptre sway?
qb.a: a) A decorated rod carried by monarchs. b) Mercy is divine, a higher quality than worldly power. c) Mercy.

qb.q: Summarize the poem ‘Quality of Mercy’.
qb.a: Mercy cannot be forced; it falls like gentle rain from heaven and blesses both giver and receiver. It is more powerful than a king’s crown and sceptre, which only cause fear. Mercy is a divine quality, the greatest virtue, which makes earthly power seem like God’s power.

qb.q: Identify the figure of speech: ‘It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven’.
qb.a: Simile.

qb.q: Identify the figure of speech: ‘It blesseth him that gives and him that takes’.
qb.a: Personification.

qb.q: Identify the figure of speech: ‘And earthly power doth then show likest God’s’.
qb.a: Simile.

qb.q: Quote from memory: ‘The quality of mercy is not strain’d’ (first four lines).
qb.a: The quality of mercy is not strain’d; It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: It blesseth him that gives, and him that takes.

qb.q: 14.1 According to the text, a king's sceptre represents
o: The spiritual and divine right of a ruler
The worldly, temporary power that brings fear and awe
The absolute mercy and kindness of a king
The decorative beauty of a royal court

qb.q: 14.2 ‘Mercy is above this sceptred sway’ because
o: mercy is a weakness that undermines a king's power
mercy is more powerful and valuable than temporary earthly authority
a king cannot rule without instilling constant dread
crowns and sceptres are easily lost in battles

qb.q: 14.3 In the given lines, the word ‘temporal’ means
o: Related to religious or sacred practices
Relating to worldly, material, or limited time

qb.q: 14.4 The statement that best captures the contrast intended by the author is
o: A king is only respected when he wears his crown.
Earthly symbols of power command fear, while mercy stands on a higher ground.
True monarchs should discard their sceptres to prove they are merciful.
Fear is a better attribute for a ruler than mercy.

qb.q: 15.1 According to the given lines, mercy descends upon the earth
o: Like a gentle rain falling from heaven
As a heavy burden on the people

qb.q: 15.2 By stating that mercy is ‘twice blest’, the author intends to state that
o: It requires two people to agree before it can happen.
It offers benefits in both this world and the afterlife.
It brings a dual benefit by rewarding both the person who shows it and the person who receives it.
It can only be granted twice by a powerful ruler.

15.4 The best scenario that demonstrates mercy as the ‘mightiest in the mightiest’ is
o: A judge imposing the maximum possible legal penalty to show authority.
A powerful ruler choosing to forgive a repentant wrong-doer when they have the absolute power to punish them.
A weak individual yielding to a demand because they have no other choice.
A wealthy merchant demanding full repayment of a debt with interest.

lessons.au: Juan A.A. Sedillo (poem: Marina de Bellagenta – ‘I Am the Land’; ‘I Draw Nourishment’ – P.T. Narasimhachar)
lessons.words: negotiation – official discussion; wretched – unpleasant; quaint – unusual and attractive in an old-fashioned way; creek – small narrow stream; orchard – land where fruit trees are grown; gnarled – twisted with hard lumps; cane – a long thin stick; innumerable – very many; kin – relatives; prune – cut branches to help growth; blossoms – flowers; preliminary – done first to prepare; broach – raise the topic; ranch – very large farm; abode – home; deed – legal agreement; ragged – torn; buena gente – good people; descendants – people related to a family from the past; sobrinos and nietos – nephews, nieces and grandchildren; ‘I am the land’: own – possess; stare – look fixedly; tickles – ploughs; chokes – suffocates; car lot eyes – looks of the people who park cars on land
lessons.notes: Story based on an actual legal case in New Mexico. Poems: ‘I Am the Land’ (Marina de Bellagenta) and ‘I Draw Nourishment’ (translated by Narasimha Murthy K.).
ab: Before you read
a. What would be the reaction of your grandfather?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: He would be very upset and refuse to sell, as the land was a family treasure inherited from his ancestors.
b. Complete the dialogue between father and grandfather.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: Father: Why is it so precious to you? Grandfather: It feeds our family and holds our history. Father: But we need the money. Grandfather: Money can come and go; the land stays with our family forever.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 1–3)
1. The old man was ………… (Fill in the blank) a. understanding b. quick c. unhurried d. witty
c. unhurried
2. Do you think the ancestors of the old man lived in Rio en Medio?
Yes. The text says his people had been in Rio en Medio for hundreds of years.
3. A word in line 4 of paragraph 1 suggests that the old man was a farmer. Pick that word.
‘tilled’ (He tilled the same land they had tilled).
4. Study the picture and describe the old man’s orchard using the words: (a small stream, unpleasant, fruit-bearing trees, old-fashioned house, attractive)

(ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಚಿತ್ರ ನೋಡಿ) Sample: A small stream runs through the attractive orchard filled with fruit-bearing trees. The old-fashioned house is quaint, though a little unpleasant in its condition.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 3–5)
5. In paragraph 2 the words ‘who’ and ‘these’ refer to ………… and ………… respectively.
Senator Catron; the people up there in the mountains.
6. Look at the picture and draw your inference about the old man’s appearance and social/living condition.
He wears an old, faded hat and long coat, and carries a walking stick. His gloves are worn and his clothes suggest that he is poor and lives simply.
images/class-10/english/c10-en-sem1-l03-old-man.webp
7. The word ‘innumerable kin’ means that the old man had a number of a. children b. trees in his orchard c. relatives d. followers e. canes.
c. relatives.
8. Why do you think the eyes of the boy are compared to gazelle? Can you write it in Kannada? (gazelle in Kannada)
The eyes of the boy are compared to a gazelle because a gazelle has large, beautiful and bright eyes. In Kannada, gazelle is ‘ಜಿಂಕೆ’.
9. How did the old man greet the people who had been waiting for him?
He bowed to all of them in the room.
10. The old man removed his hat and gloves carefully. a. Was he afraid that they would get spoiled? b. Whose style did it remind the writer of?

a. Yes, he was careful because they were old and worn. b. It reminded the writer of Charlie Chaplin’s style, as in the film where Chaplin, as a bank janitor, removed his hat and gloves in the same way.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 4–8)

1. Talk about rain and his family was ……… Tick the appropriate answers: a. to mock his large family b. to break the ice c. a custom of the Americans d. to make themselves comfortable e. to prepare everyone for the main talk f. to make everyone know that it had not rained.
b. to break the ice; e. to prepare everyone for the main talk.
2. Why do you think the story teller spoke Spanish?
Because the old man spoke Spanish, and speaking his language made him feel respected and comfortable.
3. The story teller offered the old man almost double what he had quoted earlier. Why?
The engineer found that the land extended across the river and was almost twice as large as the old man thought.
4. What was the reaction of the old man to the story teller’s offer?
He was offended. He said he did not like to be spoken to in that manner and refused the extra money, insisting on the agreed price.
5. We respect elders in many ways. For example: a. We shake hands. b. We touch their feet. c–f. Add four more ways.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: c. We greet them with folded hands. d. We offer them our seat. e. We listen to them respectfully. f. We do not interrupt them when they speak.
6. The story teller respected the old man by ………… (Fill in the blank)
addressing him as ‘Don’, a title of respect.
7a. After the findings of the engineer the offer was doubled. Did the old man raise the rate?
No. He refused more than the agreed amount.
7b. Did the story teller offer more?
Yes. He offered almost double the amount.
8. Match the following: 1. Seller 2. Some Americans 3. A young dark boy. Options: People of Spain / Follower of the old man / Buyers / The story teller / Don Anselmo.
1 – Don Anselmo; 2 – Buyers; 3 – Follower of the old man.

9. Don Anselmo took only 12 hundred dollars for the land finally because … Tick the correct answer: a. the story teller failed to convince him to take more money b. Don Anselmo was a man of principles.
b. Don Anselmo was a man of principles.
10. What did Don Anselmo do as he left the place with the money?
He shook hands all around, put on his ragged gloves, took his stick and walked out with the boy behind him.
Check your understanding (Paragraphs 7–9)
1. Fill in the blanks describing the land and house before and after it was sold: a) peeled-off plaster → replastered house; b) unpruned trees → pruned trees; c) torn fence → patched fence.
a) replastered house (after); b) unpruned trees (before); c) patched fence (after).

2. Tick the activities in which the children of Rio en Medio were involved after the Americans occupied the land: i. pruning the trees ii. renovating the house iii. playing in the orchard iv. speaking harsh words in Spanish v. plucking flowers vi. putting fences around their play area vii. laughing when spoken to viii. running around the land.
iii, v, vi, vii, viii.
3. Which of the possibilities for a week-long delay do you agree with? (deliberately delayed / was slow / was ill / was not in station)
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Accept reasoned answers. Sample: ‘was slow’, since the old man was in no hurry and had plenty of time (Paragraph 1).
4. Don Anselmo repeated certain things whenever he met the story teller and took leave. Write them down. (a. the old man shakes hands)
a. shakes hands all around; b. talks about the weather; c. wears the same faded cutaway; d. carries the same stick; e. is accompanied by the boy behind his chair.
5. ‘The Americans are good people.’ Does his remark strike you as sarcastic or sincere?
Sincere. He says it with respect and goodwill, and his later words show that he genuinely believes it.
Check your understanding (after Paragraph 12)
1. Don Anselmo sold his land but he didn’t sell his ………….
trees
2. The children of Rio en Medio were Don Anselmo’s ………… and …………
sobrinos (nephews/nieces) and nietos (grandchildren)
3. Don Anselmo inherited the house from his ………….
mother
4. According to Don Anselmo, the real owner/s of the trees was/were ……… a. the children of Rio en Medio b. Don Anselmo himself c. the Americans d. the story teller e. Don Anselmo’s ancestors
a. the children of Rio en Medio

5. Don Anselmo did not sell the trees. Why? Tick: a. Trees were like children to him. b. They were grown for the children of the next generation. c. He thought they did not belong to him but to the children. d. He had grown them in memory of his ancestors. e. He wanted his surroundings to be green.
b and c. Every child born in the village was given a tree, so the trees belonged to the children.
Think about the text
1. Don Anselmo’s appearance and manners were quite unusual. How would you support this statement?

His coat was old and faded, his gloves were torn, and his stick was the skeleton of a worn-out umbrella. Yet he bowed politely to all, removed his hat carefully, and spoke about the weather and rain before business, which was unusual.
2. Whose argument do you agree with? Don Anselmo’s or the story teller’s? Give reasons.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: I agree with Don Anselmo, because the trees were grown for the village children and had a value beyond money.
3. Don Anselmo was passionate about his land and the children of Rio en Medio. Which details support this?
He planted a tree for every child born since he took possession of the house; he refused a fortune to keep the trees for the children; and he called the children his descendants.
4. Don Anselmo’s reaction to the offer of more money was not expected. Justify this.
A poor man would normally accept more money, but he refused it, feeling insulted by the way it was offered and because he would not cheat the children’s trees.
Think about the text – Tone of the old man (paragraph 5)
a) Friend – polite / respectful
polite
b) I do not like – self-assertive
self-assertive / harsh
c) I know these – confident
confident / authoritative
d) I do not care to be insulted – firm
self-assertive / blunt
e) That is the price – authoritative
authoritative / blunt
Think about the text (Questions 6–11)
6. Why do you think the Americans wanted to buy Don Anselmo’s land?
The land had a stream, an orchard of fruit trees and a good house, so it was a fertile and attractive place to live.
7. Don Anselmo and the Americans were generous in their own ways. Comment on this.
Don Anselmo refused extra money and let the children keep the trees; the Americans offered him more money and later bought the trees from his descendants individually.
8. At last, the problem of ownership was resolved. But it took a long time. What might be the reasons? Write a paragraph.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: The trees were not included in the deed, and Don Anselmo had given them to the children of the village. The buyers had to buy each tree from Don Anselmo’s descendants, which took most of a winter.

9. Arrange the events in the order in which they occur: a. offered more money; b. children disturbed the Americans; c. Americans bought trees from descendants; d. story teller surprised by the argument; e. Don Anselmo lived in Rio en Medio; f. buyers renovated the house; g. Don Anselmo signed for 1200 dollars; h. Don Anselmo felt offended; i. occupants complained about the children.
e, a, h, d, g, f, b, i, c
10. Imagine a group of four students endorses the old man’s views and another supports the Americans. Write a paragraph on each group’s argument.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample for the old man: Land must not be sold along with what the community has grown; trees belong to people who will come after us. Sample for the Americans: They legally bought the land and its trees; the land should be used by its owners.
11. Imagine your neighbour is in a fix as the Americans were. How would you solve the problem?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: I would calmly talk to my neighbour, help him read the agreement carefully, and suggest a written agreement that clearly settles the issue.

Speak well – Task 1 (Role play) and Task 2 (Dialogue)
Task 1: Take roles and say the conversation between the old man and the story teller. Note the underlined expressions used to seek one’s opinion.
Role-play activity. Expressions to note: ‘Do you agree with the price?’, ‘What’s your opinion?’, ‘What do you think?’
Task 2: Write a dialogue using some of the phrases asking for the listener’s opinion to an imaginary offer.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Sample: A: I’m thinking of selling my bicycle for 2000 rupees. What’s your opinion? B: I think it’s a fair offer. Would you agree with this price? A: Yes, but how about waiting for a better buyer? B: Any comments? I’d sell it now.
Read and respond – Task 1 (Passage on Robert and the monkey)

1. Robert went to the other side of the road because ……… a) he wanted to help the old man b) he wanted to see why the crowd had gathered c) he was curious to watch the monkey’s tricks d) he had seen one of his friends.
b. he wanted to see why the crowd had gathered.
2. The word ‘pavement’ in the fifth line of para 1 is ……… a) a temporary tent b) a path at the side of a road for people to walk on c) a small wooden building d) a shelf on the road.
b. a path at the side of a road for people to walk on.
3. The old man let out a loud cry suddenly in order to ……… a) keep the monkey quiet b) let the crowd know his monkey was dead c) let the crowd know that he was poor d) show that he was hurt.
c. let the crowd know that he was poor.
4. Why did the old man begin to weep?
He was pretending. The monkey was not dead; he pretended to weep so that the crowd would give him money.
5. What wise thing did Robert do after he watched the monkey’s tricks for the second time?
He did not throw any money into the hat the second time. He saw through the trick and went on his way.

Understand the poem – ‘I Am the Land’
1. Who do you think is the speaker of the poem?
The land (the earth) is the speaker.
2. ‘I wait’ in line 1 suggests the feeling of a) annoyance b) patience c) disgust.
b. patience.
3. In line 2 ‘you’ is repeated. Do you think it refers to the same person?
No. It refers to different people, such as the owners and users who claim and exploit the land.
4. Bring out the contrast between the reader and the speaker as suggested in lines 4, 5 and 6.
The reader (people) shout, buy and claim the land, while the speaker (land) lies patient and waits silently.
5. ‘muddy holes’ refers to a) virtual holes b) intention of the speaker c) commotion created by the reader.
c. commotion created by the reader.
6. What does the phrase ‘car lot eyes stare’ suggest? Draw the picture if you can.
(ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಚಿತ್ರ ನೋಡಿ) It suggests the land being used as a parking lot for cars and seen only for commercial gain. Learner to draw.
7. Classify the actions: chokes, shoots, waits, shouts, sings, rejoices, destroys, plants, dances, tramples, grows, says he owns, faces the challenge, kills.
The Land: waits, grows, faces the challenge. A common man/child: plants, dances, sings, rejoices. A war-mongerer: shoots, chokes, destroys, tramples, kills, shouts, says he owns.

‘YOU CANNOT PUT A FENCE AROUND THE PLANET EARTH’.
Read and appreciate – ‘I Am the Land’
1. ‘I wait’ is repeated five times. What quality of the speaker is highlighted?
Patience and endurance, together with the land’s quiet strength.
2. Pick out figures of speech (personification).
‘A chainlink necklace chokes me now’; ‘I lie patient’; ‘tickles me, plants life’.
3. Pick out other images from the poem.
Soldiers with guns; children dancing; someone singing; fruit, grass and trees growing; muddy holes.
4. ‘YOU CANNOT PUT A FENCE AROUND THE PLANET EARTH’ – tone of weakness or self-assertion?
Self-assertion. The land declares that no one can own or confine the whole earth.

Recite and enjoy – ‘I Draw Nourishment’
Is the theme of this poem the same as that of ‘I am the land, I wait’? Who does the word ‘I’ stand for in ‘I Draw Nourishment’?
Yes, both poems speak of nature’s patience and selfless giving. The ‘I’ stands for a tree, which feeds on dirt and slush, gives shade and fruit, and never does harm.

qb.q: 18. Describe the property of Don Anselmo.
qb.a: His house was small and wretched but quaint; a little creek ran through his land; the orchard was gnarled and beautiful.

qb.q: 19. Explain briefly the appearance and manners of Don Anselmo.
qb.a: He wore an old, faded green coat and old, torn gloves; his cane was the skeleton of a worn-out umbrella. He bowed politely to all and slowly removed his hat and gloves.

qb.q: 20. How did Don Anselmo greet the guests who had been waiting for him?
qb.a: He bowed to all of them, removed his hat and gloves slowly and carefully, and handed his things to a boy standing behind his chair.

qb.q: 21. What did the Americans discover after the survey?
qb.a: He owned more than eight acres of land, extending across the river, almost twice as much as he had thought.

qb.q: 22. The storyteller offered the old man almost double what he had quoted earlier. Why?
qb.a: The survey showed Don Anselmo owned more than eight acres, which extended across the river.

qb.q: 23. What was the reaction of the old man to the storyteller’s offer?
qb.a: He hung his head in thought, stood up and stared at the story teller, feeling insulted.

qb.q: 24. Why did the old man refuse to take extra money?
qb.a: He had agreed to sell for twelve hundred dollars and was a man of principles who stuck to his word; he felt insulted by the offer.

qb.q: 25. What makes you feel that the American friends were truthful people?
qb.a: After the survey they found more land and offered double the price, showing honesty and generosity.

qb.q: 26. Why did the storyteller say the Americans were buena gente?
qb.a: Because they did not want to cheat Don Anselmo and were willing to pay him double for his land.

qb.q: 27. What makes you think Don Anselmo was a man of principles?
qb.a: He refused the offer of double money and stuck to the agreed price, and refused to sell the trees that belonged to the children.

qb.q: 28. What made the Americans complain against the children of Rio en Medio?
qb.a: The children ran around the land, played in the orchard, put up fences around their play area, plucked flowers and replied in Spanish.

qb.q: 29. Don Anselmo had concern for the children of Rio en Medio. Explain briefly.
qb.a: He had planted a tree for every child born and said the trees belonged to the children, so he refused to sell them to the Americans.

qb.q: 30. Why was the storyteller unable to convince the old man?
qb.a: Don Anselmo insisted he had sold the property, not the trees, which belonged to the children of the village.

qb.q: 31. How was the problem of ownership resolved by the Americans?
qb.a: They bought the trees individually from the descendants of Don Anselmo, that is, from each child of Rio en Medio, which took a long time.

qb.q: 32. Why did the Americans want to buy Don Anselmo’s land?
qb.a: The land had a stream, an orchard of fruit trees and a good house, which was attractive and fertile.

qb.q: 33. What changes did the Americans make in the orchard?
qb.a: They replastered the old house, pruned the trees, patched the fence and moved in for the summer.

qb.q: Don Anselmo had some peculiar manners when he visited his friends. Explain.
qb.a: He bowed to all and removed his hat and gloves slowly and carefully. He handed his things to the boy standing behind his chair, and while leaving he shook hands all around, put on his ragged gloves, took his stick and walked out with the boy.

qb.q: Don Anselmo and the Americans were generous in their own ways. Explain.
qb.a: Don Anselmo refused extra money and let the children keep the trees. The Americans, after finding more land, offered double the price and later bought the trees individually from the children, showing honesty and generosity.

qb.q: Don Anselmo’s reaction to the offer of more money was not expected. Justify.
qb.a: He had agreed to sell for twelve hundred dollars and felt insulted by the offer of double money because he stuck to his word; such refusal was not expected from a poor man.

qb.q: 1. ‘I wait’ is repeated five times. What quality of the speaker is highlighted?
qb.a: Patience and endurance, together with the land’s quiet strength.

qb.q: 2. Bring out the contrast between the speaker (land) and humans in the poem.
qb.a: The land is patient and bears all the cruelty of man, while humans claim, dig, fence and pollute the land and wage wars for it.

qb.q: 3. What activities do men do on the land, according to the poem?

qb.a: Mother Earth is the speaker. She waits patiently while people claim to own her, dig her, plant trees, grow fruit, and fence her. Soldiers come with guns and fences suffocate her like chains, yet she bears everything without complaint and mocks human greed with a tone of self-assertion.
